During our discussion today, we’ll follow the Reflect-and-Respond Dialogue protocol. This protocol helps us build meaning together rather than just sharing separate opinions. You will work in groups of four, and each round will follow the same structure:
I will ask and post the text-dependent question.
You will get two to three minutes to reread, find evidence, and write down your ideas in response.
One student will begin as the presenter and share their responses.
Each student has one minute to speak and share their responses.
The final student has 30 seconds to synthesize the group’s thinking, naming one point of agreement and one new insight.

Tree-ear’s understanding of when clay is refined enough to be used for pottery or glaze helped me understand that knowledge is gained over time (pp. 75–76). The excerpt about Tree-ear learning how to correctly cut clay from the riverbank helped me understand that skills are developed by observing, trying, failing, and refining (pp. 31–33). When someone is loyal, they show devotion or faithfulness to a person or thing. The word
is a noun that means “the condition of showing devotion or faithfulness to a person or thing.”

Tree-ear shows loyalty to Crane-man by making sure he is cared for and fed while Tree-ear goes on his journey. Tree-ear shows loyalty to Min by finishing his journey to Songdo despite a major setback.

or another text read during the unit. Across the novel, Tree-ear’s apprenticeship shows that artists and craftspeople keep traditions alive by passing down knowledge, skills, and values. As Tree-ear’s reluctant mentor, Min keeps the tradition of Goryeo celadon pottery alive by sharing with Tree-ear knowledge about refining clay to use in both the pottery and the special jade-green glaze (pp. 75–76). From observing Min, Tree-ear learns important skills like how to purify clay and how to hand mold and incise the clay with details—techniques that make Min’s pottery especially beautiful and valuable (p. 67). Tree-ear’s apprenticeship also shows that craftspeople keep their craft alive by passing on values such as hard work, perseverance, and a willingness to take risks and try new things. This is supported by Min’s efforts to learn and perfect Kang’s inlay technique. Use the Unit 2 Academic Discussion 2 Scoring Rubric to assess students’ discussion performance. standards.description: Describe how a particular story’s or drama’s plot unfolds in a series of episodes as well as how the characters respond or change as the plot moves toward a resolution.

Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.
Follow rules for collegial discussions, set specific goals and deadlines, and define individual roles as needed.
Pose and respond to specific questions with elaboration and detail by making comments that contribute to the topic, text, or issue under discussion.
Review the key ideas expressed and demonstrate understanding of multiple perspectives through reflection and paraphrasing.
Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.

By the end of the year, read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poems, in the grades 6–8 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
Determine a theme or central idea of a text and how it is conveyed through particular details; provide a summary of the text distinct from personal opinions or judgments.
Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information and evidence, paraphrasing key ideas, building on responses, and providing useful feedback.
Engage in conversational exchanges and express ideas on familiar topics by asking and answering yes‐no and wh‐ questions and responding using simple phrases.
Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information, and paraphrasing key ideas.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations using appropriate register (e.g., to reflect on multiple perspectives) using a variety of learned phrases, indirect reported speech (e.g., I heard you say X, and Gabriel just pointed out Y), as well as open responses.
